title: Care for our common home
hookLine: Pope Francis and Patriarch Bartholomew, with Protestant leaders, call Christians to care for creation
tomorrow: The priest and the big bang

lines: A LETTER THAT OPENS WITH A SONG.
cards: A pope writes a long letter, and he doesn't open it with theology.
He opens it with a song: an old Italian song by Francis of Assisi, praising God for the sun and the wind and the water, and for the earth, which Francis calls our sister and our mother.
Pope Francis took that saint's name. Now he takes the saint's song and makes it the first words of a letter about the planet. He isn't alone.
The Orthodox patriarch Bartholomew, in Constantinople, has said plainly that harming the creation is a sin. Protestant and Anglican leaders have joined their voices too.

teach.h: LAUDATO SI': PRAISE BE TO YOU.
teach.b: Our common home is the subtitle of that letter, which takes its name from the song's opening words, Laudato si', praise be to you. The idea underneath is very old.

teach.h: TO DRESS IT AND TO KEEP IT.
teach.b: In Genesis, in the King James Bible: "And the LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it." The man is a gardener before he is anything else.
And keep is a strong word in this story: a chapter later, God sets cherubims at the garden's east side "to keep the way of the tree of life." Keeping, here, is guarding.
The Psalms say whose garden it is: "The earth is the LORD's, and the fulness thereof; the world, and they that dwell therein."
On that reading, people are tenants, not owners, and that thread runs through what these church leaders say.

teach.h: THE CRY OF THE EARTH AND OF THE POOR.
teach.b: Pope Francis writes that the cry of the earth and the cry of the poor are bound together, because when land and water are spoiled, the poorest feel it first.
Patriarch Bartholomew speaks of the world as something to be received with thanks and offered back, the way bread is offered at the altar.
Protestant leaders talk about stewardship: looking after what belongs to someone else. Christians still argue, honestly, about the details: what to do, how fast, who should pay.
What they share is the starting point: the garden was handed over to be kept, not used up.

how: Some churches keep a season of prayer for creation, and congregations take it up in different ways: services, planting, cleanups, and changes to how their buildings use energy.

games.q: in Genesis 2, God takes the man and puts him in the garden of Eden. what is he there to do?
o: to use it up however he likes.
to dress it and to keep it.
games.why: "to dress it and to keep it." before anything else in the story, the man is a gardener, looking after ground that isn't his.

practice: Look around wherever you are, a tap, a light, a window, a patch of ground outside, and let your eye land on one ordinary thing you could look after a little better, something small enough that you'd actually do it.
If you pray, give thanks in the psalm's words, the earth is the Lord's; if not, hold that one thing in mind, and let these minutes be about keeping, not using.

wordCard.voice: Laudato si'. Praise be to you, the opening words of Francis of Assisi's song and the title of Pope Francis's letter calling the earth a garden to keep, not to use up.

orig.note: Hebrew: to keep, guard, watch over — the root of "to keep it" in Genesis 2:15.
